subtype: Reading the body as a signal and acting [Response]
passage:
Nitin worked at the cooperative bank in their small town and, since the spring, had also taken evening tuitions to save for his sister's college. By June, he had headaches most days, his stomach burned after meals and he woke at three every night.
His elder brother Jeevan noticed him rubbing his forehead at dinner. "How long has that been going on?"
"A while. It's nothing."
"It's not nothing if it keeps coming back."
Nitin thought about it. It was coming back. So on Saturday he went to the doctor at the town clinic, who checked him and asked about his days. He dropped the late tuition batch and told Jeevan honestly how stretched he felt. Jeevan offered to help with the college fees.
Every evening Nitin walked along the canal before dinner and turned off his phone by ten. Within a few weeks, the headaches came less often.

qa.q: Where did Nitin walk every evening?
qa.a: He walked along the canal before dinner.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he said it was nothing?
qa.a: He was probably tired and stretched but trying to brush off his worry and keep going.

qa.q: Which steps did Nitin take, and why did they help?
qa.a: He saw the doctor, dropped the late tuition batch, talked honestly with Jeevan and rebuilt rest routines, which lowered the stress his body was signalling.

qa.q: How did Jeevan respond to Nitin's honesty?
qa.a: Jeevan listened and offered to help with the college fees, sharing the load.

grounding: It shows a person who notices repeated stress symptoms and acts: seeing a doctor, reducing load, talking to someone and rebuilding rest.

subtype: Reading the body as a signal and acting [Response]
passage:
For months, Tuan ignored it. As a line cook in a busy Toronto restaurant, he worked six nights a week. First it was a tight chest after service. Then heartburn. Then his hands shook while plating. He told himself it would pass.
It didn't. It got louder. One night he had to step out into the alley, gripping the wall, heart hammering.
His flatmate Liam drove him home. "Tuan, your body's been shouting at you for months."
"I know," Tuan said quietly.
The next week he saw a doctor, who checked his heart and found it healthy, and talked with him about stress. Tuan asked his chef for five nights instead of six. He told Liam more about how he was really feeling. He started going to bed at the same time every night.
The tight chest still showed up sometimes. But now he listened to it early.

qa.q: How many nights a week did Tuan work at first?
qa.a: He worked six nights a week.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel when he admitted Liam was right?
qa.a: He felt quietly shaken and ready to accept that his body had been warning him.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Tuan do to fix it?
qa.a: Ignoring the symptoms made them louder until he had to step outside; he then saw a doctor, cut a shift, talked to Liam and fixed his sleep routine.

qa.q: How might Liam have felt driving Tuan home?
qa.a: Liam was probably scared and relieved at once, and wanted Tuan to finally take the signals seriously.

grounding: It shows how ignoring repeated stress symptoms made them louder, and how seeing a doctor, reducing load, talking and resting help.
